questions.q: What are the word parts used to build medical terms?
options: Prefix, word root, suffix and combining form vowel
questions.explain: Splitting a term into its parts reveals its meaning.
questions.evidence: Those word parts are prefix , word root , suffix , and combining form vowel

questions.q: What does the combining form oste/o mean?
questions.explain: Osteoarthritis = oste/o (bone) + arthr/o (joint) + -itis (inflammation).
questions.evidence: Oste/o is a combining form that means bone

questions.q: When you add a suffix that begins with a vowel to a combining form, what happens to the combining vowel?
questions.explain: Keep the vowel before suffixes starting with a consonant, e.g. enter/o + -logy = enterology.
questions.evidence: When combining a combining form with a suffix that begins with a vowel you drop the combining form vowel.

questions.q: What is the anatomical position?
options: Lying face down with arms by the sides
Standing upright with feet at shoulder width and parallel, toes forward
questions.explain: Directional terms are always used as if the body is in this position.
questions.evidence: is that of the body standing upright, with the feet at shoulder width and parallel, toes forward.

questions.q: What does 'superior' (or cranial) describe?
options: A position closer to the surface
A position above or higher than another part of the body
A position closer to the midline
questions.explain: Its opposite is inferior (caudal).
questions.evidence: Superior (or cranial ) describes pertaining to a position above or higher than another part of the body proper.

questions.q: What are the two basic types of tissue membranes?
options: Connective tissue membranes and epithelial membranes
questions.explain: Synovial membranes are connective; mucous and serous membranes are epithelial.
questions.evidence: There are two basic types of tissue membranes: connective tissue and epithelial membranes

questions.q: What primarily drives your need to breathe?
questions.explain: Oxygen is critical for cells, but rising CO2 triggers breathing.
questions.evidence: it is the accumulation of carbon dioxide that primarily drives your need to breathe.

questions.q: Which organs are the accessory organs of digestion?
questions.explain: Food doesn't pass through them, but their roles are vital.
questions.evidence: The liver, pancreas, and gallbladder are considered accessory digestive organs

questions.q: How do electronic health records (EHRs) compare with electronic medical records (EMRs)?
questions.explain: EHRs are designed to share information across providers.
questions.evidence: While often used interchangeably, EHRs are broader than electronic medical records (EMRs).

questions.q: How can EHRs lead to better patient outcomes?
options: By exposing potential safety problems when they occur
questions.explain: Alerts and complete histories help providers avoid serious consequences.
questions.evidence: EHRs can expose potential safety problems when they occur, helping providers avoid more serious consequences for patients and leading to better patient outcomes.

questions.q: What is the main U.S. federal law that protects health information?
questions.explain: HIPAA sets privacy and security rules for health information.
questions.evidence: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) is the main Federal law that protects health information.

questions.q: What is the lamina propria?
options: The outer layer of the skin
The connective tissue beneath a mucous membrane's epithelium that supports it
questions.explain: Its name literally means 'own layer'.
questions.evidence: The underlying connective tissue, called the lamina propria

questions.q: What is a serous membrane (serosa)?
options: A membrane covered in dead keratinised cells
A membrane made only of fat
An epithelial membrane of mesothelium supported by connective tissue
questions.explain: Serous membranes line the anterior (ventral) body cavity.
questions.evidence: is an epithelial membrane composed of mesodermally derived epithelium called the mesothelium that is supported by connective tissue

questions.q: What is the trachea made of?
options: 16–20 stacked C-shaped pieces of hyaline cartilage joined by dense connective tissue
questions.explain: The cartilage rings keep the airway open.
questions.evidence: The trachea is formed by 16 to 20 stacked, C-shaped pieces of hyaline cartilage that are connected by dense connective tissue.

questions.q: What are the main functions of the respiratory system?
options: Supplying oxygen, removing carbon dioxide and helping maintain acid-base balance
questions.explain: Oxygen supports cellular respiration; CO2 is the waste product.
questions.evidence: function primarily to provide oxygen to body tissues for cellular respiration, remove the waste product carbon dioxide, and help to maintain acid-base balance

questions.q: Into which three regions is the pharynx divided?
questions.explain: Each region connects to a different neighbouring structure.
questions.evidence: The pharynx is divided into three major regions: the nasopharynx , the oropharynx , and the laryngopharynx

questions.q: Where does the trachea branch into the right and left primary bronchi?
questions.explain: The bronchi keep branching into the bronchial tree.
questions.evidence: The trachea branches into the right and left primary bronchi at the carina

questions.q: How much does living with a smoker raise a non-smoker's risk of lung cancer?
questions.explain: Second-hand smoke is a significant health risk.
questions.evidence: the risk of developing lung cancer is increased by up to 30 percent in nonsmokers who live with an individual who smokes in the house

questions.q: What are people with COPD advised to do?
options: Avoid sick people, get the flu shot and reduce exposure to pollution and smoke
questions.explain: Infections and irritants can make COPD much worse.
questions.evidence: Clients with COPD are advised to avoid people who are sick, get the flu shot and reduce their exposure to pollution and cigarette smoke.

questions.q: How are fast-acting drugs for an asthma attack usually given?
questions.explain: Inhalers deliver the drug straight to the airways.
questions.evidence: Short-term, fast-acting drugs that are used to treat an asthma attack are typically administered via an inhaler.

questions.q: What is the visceral pleura?
options: The layer lining the chest wall
The pleural layer on the surface of the lungs that lines their fissures
questions.explain: The parietal pleura is the outer layer.
questions.evidence: The visceral pleura is the layer that is superficial to the lungs, and extends into and lines the lung fissures

questions.q: What is the pericardium?
options: The tough membrane sac that surrounds the heart
The muscle layer of the heart
questions.explain: The heart sits in its own space, the pericardial cavity.
questions.evidence: a tough membrane known as the pericardium, or pericardial sac

questions.q: What is the base of the heart?
options: Its superior surface, where the great vessels attach
questions.explain: The great vessels carry blood to and from the heart.
questions.evidence: are attached to the superior surface of the heart, which is called the base

questions.q: How many layers make up the wall of the heart?
questions.explain: The epicardium, myocardium and endocardium.
questions.evidence: The walls of the heart consist of three layers

questions.q: What is heart failure?
options: A blocked artery in the brain
The heart's inability to pump enough blood to meet the body's needs
questions.explain: It can result from conditions such as cardiomyopathy.
questions.evidence: Heart failure is defined as the inability of the heart to pump enough blood to meet the needs of the body.

questions.q: Why can cardiomyopathy lead to heart failure?
options: The diseased heart muscle cannot contract and pump blood properly
questions.explain: The myocardium is the heart's pumping muscle.
questions.evidence: Because the myocardium is responsible for contracting and pumping blood, patients with cardiomyopathy experience impaired heart function which may lead to heart failure.

questions.q: What is hypertrophy?
options: An increase in muscle cells, for example as a result of exercise
questions.explain: In the heart it can be healthy (exercise) or a sign of disease.
questions.evidence: exercise results in an increase in muscle cells called hypertrophy

questions.q: What is the oral vestibule?
options: The pocket between the gums and teeth and the cheeks and lips
questions.explain: It is the outermost part of the mouth.
questions.evidence: The pocket-like part of the mouth that is framed on the inside by the gums and teeth, and on the outside by the cheeks and lips is called the oral vestibule

questions.q: What is the fauces?
options: The opening between the oral cavity and the throat
questions.explain: Think of it like a kitchen 'faucet'.
questions.evidence: the opening between the oral cavity and throat (oropharynx) is called the fauces

questions.q: What forms the hard palate?
questions.explain: Its bony structure is why it is called 'hard'.
questions.evidence: It is created by the maxillary and palatine bones of the skull and, given its bony structure, is known as the hard palate.

questions.q: What is bilirubin?
options: A digestive enzyme made in the stomach
The main bile pigment, a waste product from old red blood cells
A type of white blood cell
questions.explain: It forms when the spleen removes old or damaged red blood cells.
questions.evidence: the main bile pigment, is a waste product produced when the spleen removes old or damaged red blood cells from the circulation

questions.q: Where is the gallbladder located?
options: In a shallow area on the back of the liver's right lobe
questions.explain: It is about 8–10 cm long.
questions.evidence: is nested in a shallow area on the posterior aspect of the right lobe of the liver

questions.q: What is ingestion?
options: The absorption of nutrients in the intestine
The entry of food into the alimentary canal through the mouth
questions.explain: It is the first of the digestive processes.
questions.evidence: refers to the entry of food into the alimentary canal through the mouth

questions.q: How does electronic health information exchange help patient records?
options: It can greatly improve their completeness
questions.explain: Providers see past history and current medications.
questions.evidence: which can greatly improve the completeness of a patient

questions.q: How is information sent between providers who already know and trust each other?
options: Over the internet in an encrypted, secure and reliable way
questions.explain: Security protects patients' sensitive information.
questions.evidence: This information is sent over the internet in an encrypted, secure, and reliable way amongst health care professionals who already know and trust each other.

questions.q: How can EHRs help providers diagnose problems sooner?
options: By giving reliable access to a patient's complete health information
questions.explain: A comprehensive picture speeds up diagnosis.
questions.evidence: With EHRs, providers can have reliable access to a patient’s complete health information.

questions.q: Besides improving diagnosis, what can EHRs reduce or even prevent?
questions.explain: Fewer errors means better patient outcomes.
questions.evidence: Electronic health records (EHRs) can improve the ability to diagnose diseases and reduce—even prevent—medical errors, improving patient outcomes.
